newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Brierley's Australian oil trust float disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Brierley's Australian oil trust float disappoints.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd's attempt to reap A$220 million (US$164 million) through a float of its main Australian oil asset suffered another blow on Monday when the float vehicle traded below its issue price on its first day.
The New Zealand investment group's plan to sell 44 million units in the Bass Strait Oil Trust at A$5 a unit floundered in late June when it was forced to take up a 25 percent shortfall.
Analysts said institutional investors in particular were sceptical about the projections for the Bass Strait trust and had stayed away in droves from the float.
"The forecast oil production profile was reasonably optimistic," said Wilson HTM oil analyst John Webby.
"We recommended that we believed there was better value elsewhere," said Webby.
The cool reaction from brokers and institutional investors was reflected in the trust's lacklustre first day of trade, with less than 100,000 units trading at prices between A$4.75 and A$5.00 a unit.
Brierley's Australian unit, Australian Consolidated Investments Ltd (ACIL), launched the float of the trust in May, hoping to make a profit of about A$110 million from the deal.
But it closed on June 20 under-subscribed by 11 million shares, forcing ACIL to take up the A$55 million worth of units left on the shelf.
The trust owns just over half of an overall 2.5 percent royalty stream from Australia's largest petroleum production area, the Bass Strait oil and gas project between Victoria and Tasmania.

The float vehicle owns the part of the overall royalty known as the "Weeks" royalty, named after consultant Lewis Weeks who discovered the Bass Strait reserves in 1966 for the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP).
The Bass Strait project accounted for about 40 percent of Australia's oil production in 1996.
The float was structured so that the units were to be redeemed progressively over their 10 year life through 20 equal half-yearly repayments of 25 cents each.
After this 10 year period, the ownership of the "Weeks" royalty reverts to ACIL.
This structure effectively meant investors were buying a bond-like instrument leveraged to the oil price with a projected after-tax yield of about 10.5 percent.
Analysts said institutional investors in particular were wary of buying the units because they limited the prospect for growth, but still carried the oil price risk.
"If you're taking a punt on the oil price, you'd be better off buying an oil stock which gives you the extra chance of growth through new discoveries," said one Sydney analyst.
The unusual structure of the units and their slowly diminishing value because of their capital repayments had also made investors wary, analysts said.
"Holding a particular stock or equity that has a diminishing value doesn't have any attractions," one said.
Analysts and brokers said the 11 million units held by ACIL would also hang over the market, depressing the price in the short term at least.
The float's underperfomance is also emphasised by the general market's 7.2 percent rally since the A$5 a unit price was set on May 19.
Bass Strait was down 10 cents or two percent on its issue price at A$4.90 just ahead of the close on its first day of trade.
